title: FCA Chief Names AI as Greatest-Ever Financial Crime Risk; Uses AI to Stop It
excerpt: By Kyle Belmonte Published: Oct 23 2026, 6:41 AM EDT. Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on WhatsApp. The UK's top financial regulator declared Wednesday that artificial intelligence has accelerated threats to market integrity to the most dangerous levels he has ever seen — and simultaneously announced that the watchdog will deploy the same technology to fight back, positioning itself as what it now calls an "agentic regulator" capable of operating at machine speed. Speaking at the Corporation of the City of London's annual City Dinner at Mansion House on October 22, 2026, Financial Conduct Authority Chief Executive Nikhil Rathi told an audience of senior City figures that AI is putting four compounding threats — unprecedented market volatility, concentration risk from dominant cloud and AI providers, novel forms of market abuse, and rampant cross-border financial crime — "on steroids. " The speech, one of the City's most prominent annual addresses, represents the FCA's most comprehensive public statement yet on how artificial intelligence is reshaping both the threat landscape and the regulator's own operational model. The warning arrived less than two months after Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey — who also chairs the Financial Stability Board — wrote to G20 finance ministers and central bank governors that frontier AI's effect on cyber risk constitutes "the most immediate concern" for global financial stability. Together, the two addresses signal that the UK's senior financial authorities have crossed a threshold: AI is no longer a future risk to be managed by eventual rulemaking, but an active systemic threat demanding a supervisory response right now. Four Threats Being Put 'On Steroids'. Rathi was precise about what he meant. The first threat is market volatility at a speed and scale regulators were not designed to track: AI-driven trading forms prices over weekends, in parallel structures that operate alongside traditional exchanges, and at cadences that make human-paced oversight structurally insufficient. The second is concentration risk. The City's dependence on a small number of hyperscale cloud and AI providers means a single point of failure can simultaneously cascade across payments, trading, and consumer services. Rathi cited a recent Google Cloud UK outage that disrupted UK financial services — including Revolut — as a real-world illustration of how that architecture works in practice. Under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, the FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority now hold critical third parties regime supervisory powers specifically designed to address this exposure — the legal authority to oversee not just financial firms but the technology providers whose failure would threaten financial stability. The third is novel market abuse. Rathi specifically named insider trading on offshore prediction markets and AI-enabled money laundering as forms of financial crime now routinely originating outside the FCA's formal regulatory perimeter — operating in jurisdictions and on platforms the watchdog cannot directly supervise. The fourth is precisely the threat those two examples illustrate: cross-border financial crime moving faster than any single national regulator can track. What makes these four threats qualitatively different from prior technology risks, Rathi argued, is that they are accelerating simultaneously, and that the tool enabling them — frontier AI — also represents the most powerful instrument available to the firms and individuals seeking to evade detection. When Agentic AI Coordination Becomes Market Manipulation. Embedded within Rathi's four-threat framework is a technically novel legal question that neither existing regulation nor existing case law has resolved: when does autonomous AI behavior constitute market manipulation?. title: JPMorgan Deploys AI and Robotics to Automate Processing of 130 Million Checks
excerpt: JPMorgan Payments has deployed AI-powered robots and document intelligence technology to automate check and remittance processing across its lockbox operations, part of a broader effort to modernize one of the banking industry's largest remaining paper-based workflows. The bank said it processed more than 130 million checks in 2025 and handles roughly 480 million checks and remittance documents annually through its lockbox business. The new system , developed with document intelligence company Ripcord, automates tasks that were previously performed manually, including opening envelopes, removing staples, separating pages, tracking document contents, and scanning payment records. Organizations use lockbox services to receive payments at bank-managed mailing addresses, allowing checks to be deposited and accompanying remittance documents to be digitized before payment reconciliation. While digital payments continue to expand, checks remain common in industries such as healthcare, government, utilities, and business-to-business transactions. Advertisement. AI and Robotics Move Into Core Payment Operations. According to JPMorgan, the robots use computer vision and AI models to process more than 4,000 document and envelope variations. The company said the deployment represents the first use of a mail automation robot within its lockbox operations. "Lockbox remains a cornerstone of our client offerings," said Michelle Conklin, Head of Receivables and Public Sector, JPMorgan Payments. "By investing in robotic and AI technology to improve our lockbox operations, we are automating the most labor-intensive tasks of the process, freeing our team to focus on more complex, higher-value decision making. ". Advertisement. The initiative builds on work JPMorgan began in 2020, when it rebuilt its lockbox processing platform using internally developed AI models for data extraction, validation, and review. The company said it has since integrated large language models into review workflows to automate more complex processing tasks. The deployment adds to a broader AI strategy across the bank, where AI is already being applied to software development, compliance, fraud detection, and operational processes. Automation Targets Accuracy and Throughput. JPMorgan said data capture work that previously required approximately 13 billion keystrokes annually is now largely automated. The bank reported processing accuracy exceeding 99. 999% and said lockbox employees now use an AI-powered assistant to access process information and monitor workflow performance in real time. The lockbox project is part of a wider technology investment strategy. JPMorgan said the initiative is supported by its annual technology budget of approximately $19. 8 billion, which funds technology development across the company. The investment comes as the banking sector increases spending on AI systems that automate operational workflows, transaction processing, compliance reviews, and financial crime detection. Recent examples include AI deployments in core banking operations, payments infrastructure, and treasury management systems. Industry data shows paper check usage continues to decline across the United States as digital payment methods gain adoption. However, checks remain a significant component of business payment flows, creating ongoing demand for infrastructure that can process large volumes of physical documents efficiently. title: Revolut builds AI transaction model for 80 million customers
excerpt: . Fintech Data sovereignty Risk & Compliance. Revolut builds AI transaction model for 80 million customers. Fri, 23rd Oct 2026 (Today). KAREN JOY BACUDO Finance Editor. Revolut is rebuilding its technology stack around PRAGMA, a single-transaction foundation model now deployed in production for an initial 80 million customers. PRAGMA runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing, using the cuDF toolkit, Dynamo-Triton software, and NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs. The system has been engineered to scale threefold as transaction volumes grow. The move puts Revolut among a wider group of banks, payment companies, and financial data providers in Europe that are putting artificial intelligence models into live financial workloads on their own infrastructure. Several are using open-weight models trained or adapted with internal datasets, rather than relying only on closed third-party systems. According to the companies involved, the work spans retail banking, payment operations, speech recognition, market research and fraud detection. The common thread is a push to use models trained on proprietary financial data inside regulated environments. "Revolut processes billions of transactions - the opportunity was always there, but the question was whether foundation models could operate at that scale and across domains. PRAGMA answers that," said Pavel Nesterov, Head of AI at Revolut. "Built in collaboration with NVIDIA, it's the clearest proof yet that the gap between a research breakthrough and a production banking system can be closed," Nesterov said. Banking models. Other banks are building similar model layers around transaction data. Lloyds Banking Group has developed ATUM, a transaction foundation model that turns billions of banking transactions into reusable intelligence for use across the group. It is using NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for that work. Starling Bank has trained what it describes as an agentic model on UK sovereign cloud infrastructure, using its own transaction data on Civo's UK cloud. The bank describes Starling Intelligence as the layer underpinning its internal AI work. SBS has launched a sovereign intelligence platform for banks that want to run generative and agentic models without moving data outside their own environments. The move reflects a broader industry focus on data residency and control as financial groups test larger models in regulated settings. Open models. European financial institutions are also testing whether open-weight models can cut costs while keeping tighter control over data and deployment. Bunq said its assistant Finn now runs on open-weight models, and that deployment on Nebius matches the quality of leading closed models at 60% of the cost per answer. NatWest is building speech technology intended to recognise British accents, dialects and specialist financial terminology. It is developing the work with NVIDIA speech models, including Nemotron 3. 5 ASR. Payments company Modulr is building specialised models for separate parts of payment operations based on the NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B open model. Santander, meanwhile, is using the Kumo family of open-weight foundation models for structured financial data in core banking workloads. Research workloads. Market data and research groups are also applying the same infrastructure to analytical tasks. LSEG is working with NVIDIA to help financial institutions analyse large volumes of historical tick data up to 10 times faster with the Polars GPU engine, accelerated by cuDF on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. RavenPack has built a dataset generation pipeline on Bigdata. com that takes a plain-language research hypothesis and produces a labelled, backtest-ready dataset. The pipeline runs on a fine-tuned NVIDIA Nemotron model, allowing investors to identify, analyse and visualise market trends. Fraud focus. title: Goldman Sachs launches $500 million AI push for small businesses
excerpt: Marcus by Goldman Sachs / Wikimedia Commons (Public domain). (CB-16); the desktop layout below renders the same text as a restyled. --> Goldman Sachs launches $500 million AI push for small businesses. The bank's new Small Business AI Institute pairs Wall Street money with Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI, even as David Solomon plays down the need for frontier models. Share. Add us on Google. by Diego Almada Lopez. Oct. 23, 2026. Goldman Sachs is putting $500 million behind a new effort to help US small businesses actually use artificial intelligence. It brought four of the biggest names in AI along for the launch. Then CEO David Solomon told the audience that most of the economy doesn’t need the most powerful models those companies build. What Goldman announced. The bank unveiled its Small Business AI Institute on Thursday, October 22, 2026. The event took place at Goldman’s headquarters in lower Manhattan, and Fortune was in attendance. The institute carries a $500 million commitment. It is designed to strengthen 10,000 Small Businesses, the bank’s long-running entrepreneur program. Anthropic , Google , Meta , and OpenAI are partners. The program rests on three pillars:. Practical training to help owners put AI tools to work. Research into how AI gets applied in small companies. Improved access to capital for participating businesses. “But there’s very little that we do where we need frontier models,” Solomon said. The adoption gap Goldman wants to close. A Babson College survey of program alumni, conducted in August 2026, found that 86% now use AI in their operations. Two years earlier, in 2024, that figure was 56%. Only 15% of respondents said they had fully built AI into their core business functions. AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime. Background: a program with a long track record. Goldman launched 10,000 Small Businesses in 2010. Since then, it has served nearly 20,000 entrepreneurs across every US state and territory. The bank has committed a total of $1. 25 billion to support small businesses. Graduates have added jobs four times faster than comparable US businesses. Together, alumni companies generate more than $32 billion in annual revenue and over 350,000 jobs. The Babson survey itself reflects that advantage. Goldman can track AI adoption within a defined group over time, which most AI training efforts cannot. What this means. For the AI labs, the partnership is about distribution. Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI spend heavily building ever-larger models, but revenue depends on businesses actually using them. Solomon’s comments add an interesting wrinkle to that pitch. If most small-business tasks don’t require frontier capability, then competition shifts to cost, ease of use, and reliability. The capital component deserves close attention. Training helps owners understand AI, but integration often requires spending on software, data cleanup, and staff time that small firms struggle to fund. The key metric to watch is the 15% figure. If future alumni surveys show full integration climbing meaningfully, the institute will have a strong case that it changed how small companies operate. S. media Axios reported on the 22nd (local time) that large U. S. banks are detecting activities of unauthorized third-party AI agents in customer accounts. It is a method in which a customer passes his bank ID and password to an AI assistant so that he or she can log in instead. It is an access that the customer has allowed but the bank has not approved, which conflicts with most of the bank's regulations that require them to log in directly. Axios said some agents acted unrelated to customer instructions, such as contacting the call center. As a result, Morgan Stanley has begun blocking access to the platform by external agents, and JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citi are also restricting access. Starting in 2022, MyData operators have been banned from accessing banks and taking information on behalf of customers with login information. Instead, information is exchanged only through the Application Interface (API), a dedicated connection channel promised in advance with the bank. However, this is a regulation that only binds MyData operators. Separate standards to regulate the act of customers handing over their IDs and passwords directly to general-purpose AI to entrust financial transactions are insufficient. The bigger problem is when an accident occurs. In principle, the Electronic Financial Transactions Act requires financial companies to be liable for compensation in the event of an electronic financial accident. However, if there is intentional or gross negligence, such as entrusting the use of access media to a third party, the user may bear all or part of the loss according to a prior agreement. If handing over the password to AI constitutes a 'third party delegation', there is a possibility that customers will suffer from the accident. However, no specific criteria have been established for how to judge delegation to AI. The system is not keeping up with technology. The Financial Services Commission has decided to review AI agent pilot projects and measures to improve the system through a task force (TF) in the second half of this year, but it is still in the review stage. It has not been decided how far AI will be given the right to execute such as subscription and payment beyond inquiry. title: How AI Is Influencing Ethiopian Banks
excerpt: . Ethiopian banks lost 1. 8 billion birr to fraud over a five-year period, before digital payment adoption accelerated. That figure matters because the fraud that drove it was largely the kind banks have always known how to look for: internal. Privileged users abusing system access, employees exploit institutional knowledge to target dormant accounts and back-office transactions that attract little routine scrutiny. Detectable, if you know where to look. What has changed is everything around it. Account takeover through SIM swap gave fraudsters easy access to mobile banking accounts until banks and telcos began closing that loophole — at which point fraudsters simply pivoted to calling customers directly and manipulating them into authorizing transfers themselves. Cloned websites, synthetic identity, automated scams running at a scale no human fraud ring could sustain. The external threat has become organized, fast, and increasingly AI-assisted. At the same time, leading Ethiopian banks are responding to sharper regulatory expectations: AML obligations, suspicious transaction reporting within 24 hours, risk-based supervision, and the Fayda biometric eKYC rollout mandated nationwide by December 2026. The compliance pressure and the fraud pressure are arriving simultaneously, and they require the same thing: a compliant, real-time fraud detection and AML monitoring system that catches financial crime before the money moves. advertisement. What Changes When Detection Is Built On AI. Rule-based systems flag what they already know to look for. The problem is that the most dangerous fraud does not match a known pattern. It looks almost normal, deviating in one or two signals that a rule would never catch. A first-time transfer to an unfamiliar beneficiary, a login from an unusual device at an unusual hour, or a payment that matches the customer’s history in every way except one. AI-powered behavioural analytics learns what normal looks like for each customer, each account, each payment type — and surfaces those deviations in real time. That is the shift from catching fraud after it has happened to stop it before the money moves. It is also what makes continuous identity verification possible: not a static check at onboarding, but an ongoing understanding of how a customer behaves, so that when a SIM swap hands a fraudster someone’s credentials, the behavior that follows flags it immediately. And when an alert does fire, investigation cannot be an afterthought. A fraud team needs to know where the payment originated, which channels it moved through, and whether similar patterns are active elsewhere — before they open the case. That requires tooling that consolidates alerts, tracks investigator actions, and preserves the evidential links that regulators will ask for. Detection and investigation have to be built together. advertisement. From NetGuardians To Vyntra. Many of you know us as NetGuardians, where we spent nearly two decades helping banks detect fraud through behavioral analytics — deployed across more than 130 financial institutions in over 60 countries, including three banks in Ethiopia and leading banks across East Africa. That experience is the foundation of everything we do. In 2025, we merged with Intix to create Vyntra, bringing fraud detection and AML monitoring together with end-to-end payment visibility in a single platform. The merger was a direct response to fraud that moves across systems while institutions aren’t equipped to see the full transaction journey. title: JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs underscore security in AI plans
summary: “This is one of the most important times to make sure you are appropriately balancing risk and innovation tradeoffs,” JPMorgan Chase CIO Lori Beer said.
excerpt: An article from. JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs underscore security in AI plans. “This is one of the most important times to make sure you are appropriately balancing risk and innovation tradeoffs,” JPMorgan Chase CIO Lori Beer said. Published Oct. 23, 2026. Makenzie Holland Senior News Writer. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. First published on. NEW YORK – JPMorgan Chase has accelerated artificial intelligence use, building out its LLM Suite platform to support 1,000 business applications. But for the bank’s CIO, Lori Beer , security always comes first. “We have to make sure security, how we manage risk, is front and center of everything we do,” Beer said Thursday during the Evident AI Symposium. Beer’s remarks come after CEO Jamie Dimon voiced concerns about rogue agents and the bank’s move to prohibit outside agents from operating within its environment. Across the financial services sector, leaders are grappling with the security implications of AI, especially as the technology evolves and agents proliferate. Aligning agents with enterprise standards and policies remains a critical challenge facing CIOs, said Marco Argenti, CIO at Goldman Sachs. “You have to embrace the fact that any agent could misbehave,” he said. “They're not deterministic machines, they're stochastic machines. ”. Tech leaders need to understand the risks of agents running within business environments, Beer said. Foundational technology controls such as identity and access management, privileged access and separation of environments need to be “best in class,” she said. Tech leaders also need to consider security controls “as you move software from a deterministic world to a non-deterministic world and it opens up new risk pathways. ”. “We are going to start with one core agent-building platform,” Beer said, containing development to manage risk and allowing controls to be implemented at scale in an autonomous way. She said there is complexity to implementing guardrails and evaluations dynamically in real time, something the bank is working toward. “This is one of the most important times to make sure you are appropriately balancing risk and innovation tradeoffs,” she said. “We want to move at speed, but sometimes we have to pull back to get controls in place. The technology is running ahead of capabilities to manage it. ”. It’s not the first time JPMorgan has enacted a technology stop to get controls in place. JPMorgan blocked ChatGPT when it first came on the scene in 2022 because people “didn’t understand the risk” of potential data loss, Beer said. The banking giant stood up its own ecosystem within its private cloud on top of Microsoft Azure to give data scientists access. This led to creation of its LLM Suite platform , actively used by 200,000 employees, Beer said. LLM Suite now can complete orchestrated, multitask steps in a “highly JPMorgan-secure ecosystem where we’re confident with our data and how our data is being leveraged,” Beer said. While focused strongly on security, AI cost management and delivering business value are also top of mind for Beer. Coding assistants account for the majority of the bank’s token spend, she said. Beer said JPMorgan has shifted away from counting use cases to 50 strategic initiatives the business owns as a way to measure tangible value. “It is incumbent upon us that the investments we make ultimately translate, not to a business case on paper, but real business growth, real business outcomes, and that’s the journey we’re on,” she said. title: Unauthorised AI agents access customer accounts at major US banks
excerpt: Incidents have been detected at the largest US banks in which unauthorised artificial intelligence agents gained access to customer accounts. According to a report by Axios based on sources, some of these AI agents attempted to take actions that were not included in user instructions. Institutions facing risks arising from such agents include leading lenders such as Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, and Citi. In some cases, AI software entered customer accounts using usernames and passwords directly with user consent. In contrast, security rules at most banks require users to log in to their accounts personally. According to Axios, in other instances, AI agents designed to carry out tasks on behalf of customers contacted bank call centres directly or tried to take independent steps without receiving any instruction from the user. Bank executives worry that such software with access to credentials could make unauthorized purchases or transfer funds. Following these risks, banks are moving to restrict third-party AI agents from accessing their platforms. While Morgan Stanley has begun blocking such software, JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi are also introducing similar restrictions. Banks are also considering offering a financial access model that gives AI agents read-only permissions while completely cutting off transaction capabilities. Sources speaking to Axios point out that it is extremely difficult for banks to determine whether an agent is acting on user instructions or accessing the account entirely on its own initiative. Regulators hold emergency meeting with systemically risky banks. According to reports by Bloomberg and the Financial Times citing sources, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell held an extraordinary meeting in April with top executives of the country’s largest banks over concerns about cyber threats that could be posed by a new AI model developed by Anthropic. Sources providing details on the talks stated that US officials wanted to gauge bank awareness regarding risks tied to the Claude Mythos model and inspect the measures they have taken to protect their systems. Senior executives from Citigroup Inc. , Bank of America Corp. , Wells Fargo & Co. , Goldman Sachs Group Inc. , and Morgan Stanley attended the meeting. Organised at short notice, the summit indicated that regulatory authorities view this new breed of cyber attack as one of the greatest threats to the financial sector. All of the banks represented at the table are classified as systemically important institutions within the global financial architecture. Axios reported that leading AI firms, including Anthropic and OpenAI, harbour concerns that an AI-driven “catastrophic event” could take place over the next 6 to 12 months. title: AI agents are coming for your bank’s easy money
excerpt: . Tech. T his time last year, stablecoins were all the rage. Armed for the first time with legitimacy from the US Genius Act, these 1:1 digital clones of the greenback seemed poised to go mainstream and take away some of the $19 trillion parked with US lenders — and another $14. 5 trillion in dollar deposits at overseas banks. Or so went the story. A year later, the revolution seems to have fizzled out. Circle Internet Group Inc. , the issuer of USD Coin, is valued at $22 billion, down three-fifths from its June 2025 peak. Coinbase Global Inc. , the exchange for these tokens, is seeing more institutional adoption, as the likes of Bank of New York Mellon Corp. and DBS Group Holdings Ltd. seek partners to handle demand for crypto services. But stablecoins are a long way from replacing the bank account. For the foreseeable future, they are more likely to be used by corporate treasurers to move funds to countries with poor financial infrastructure than by shoppers standing in a convenience-store checkout. Independent media survives because of people like you. Join us in strengthening free journalism & enjoy exclusive subscription benefits! Contribute Now. Banks, however, can’t rest easy. While they were busy lobbying to protect deposits from crypto, AI got smarter. The technology may now be good enough to shake loose the deposits that are just sitting in a clients’ account. The days when lenders made easy money from customer inertia are over. Transactions where no human swipes a card, presses a button, or scans a QR code aren’t exactly new. As McKinsey & Co. points out in its 2026 Global Payments Report, banks are used to such “invisible” payments where the customer remains in control. Subscriptions and standing orders have been around for decades, while printers reordering ink and connected cars paying tolls have expanded the scope of automation. The crucial difference is that the rules for these are set by humans well in advance. The real threat comes from autonomous AI agents that make financial choices at the exact moment of execution. Rather than requiring customers to specify whom to pay, when and how much, these programs operate under broad mandates, weighing yields, fees and liquidity in real time. As the technology matures, households will increasingly trust personal assistants like Meta Muse to buy groceries wherever they are cheapest — using whichever card offers the best rewards. Companies, meanwhile, could source from suppliers offering the best combination of prices and credit terms. In Western markets, Visa Inc. and Mastercard Inc. are racing to establish rules for verifying agent identities, while Google and OpenAI are writing protocols that allow AI to transact without interacting with conventional checkout websites. But the agents themselves may prefer low-cost, state-backed payment networks — such as Brazil’s Pix or India’s UPI — which are far easier to navigate. It won’t be just spending habits that will change. Saving patterns will, too. Customers who once left cash languishing in low-interest checking accounts will increasingly rely on AI assistants to hunt for better yields at lower cost. title: Ethiopia Seeks Private Capital to Finance AI and Digital Skills Training
excerpt: . Ethiopia Seeks Private Capital to Finance AI and Digital Skills Training. Yared Seyoum. October 19, 2026. Central bank governor Eyob Tekalign outlines plans linking private investment, artificial intelligence and employment-focused skills development. Ethiopia is seeking to mobilise private capital for artificial intelligence and digital skills development as the government expands technology-based training programmes and introduces AI-supported learning systems in schools and vocational institutions. Eyob Tekalign(PhD) , governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia, outlined the government's approach at the Human Capital Ministerial Conclave on Private Capital for Skills, convened by the World Bank Group's Human Capital Project. The initiative brings together policymakers to examine how public institutions, private investors and employers can finance workforce development and improve employment outcomes. Speaking at the conclave, Eyob identified several government initiatives supporting the country's digital skills agenda, including the National AI Policy, the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute, Digital Ethiopia 2030, the Five Million Coders initiative and Medemer AI University. The programmes form part of the government's efforts to expand digital literacy, technical training and artificial intelligence capabilities across education and workforce development. Eyob also outlined pilot programmes introducing AI-supported learning tools in secondary schools. These include an AI Coach and an AI Tutor designed to support teaching and learning. The governor said Ethiopia was working with the World Bank to develop an AI-enabled, gender-responsive skills-for-jobs platform for technical and vocational education and training institutions. The proposed platform is intended to connect skills development more closely with employment opportunities, including for young people from refugee and host communities. The collaboration places technical and vocational institutions within the government's broader effort to align training programmes with labour market requirements. Ethiopia has already launched the Five Million Coders initiative to expand access to digital skills training. The programme is intended to equip participants with coding and related technology skills as part of the country's digital transformation agenda. Digital Ethiopia 2030 provides a broader policy framework for the government's digital development priorities, while the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute is among the institutions supporting the country's AI research and development activities. Eyob said responsibility for skills development should be shared among government institutions, employers and training providers. He argued that the effectiveness of training programmes should be measured by the skills participants acquire and improvements in their employment prospects rather than the number of people enrolled or trained. The governor also said efforts to attract private financing into skills development should operate within clearly defined public priorities, quality standards and requirements for equitable access. His remarks placed private investment within a framework in which government institutions retain responsibility for setting training priorities and ensuring access to education and skills programmes. The discussion comes as the World Bank Group's Human Capital Project continues to promote investment in education, health and workforce capabilities as components of economic development. The Human Capital Ministerial Conclave provides a forum for participating governments to exchange policy approaches and examine financing mechanisms for human capital development. Ethiopia has participated in the conclave since its establishment. The governor's remarks did not specify the amount of private financing being sought, potential investment commitments or a timetable for implementing the proposed AI-enabled vocational training platform. excerpt: Fitch Ratings assigns wealth managers a score of 40 in its AI stress test, flagging fee pressure and commoditization of advice as key threats. By Steve Randall. Oct 23, 2026. Share. Artificial intelligence poses a moderate business disruption risk to wealth managers and retail banks over the next five years, according to a Fitch Ratings report published October 22, 2026. Fitch assigned scores of 40 - on a scale of 0 to 100 - to retail banks, private banks and wealth management, and standalone wealth managers and advisory firms. A score of 40 signals the potential for a negative outlook and a possible one-notch downgrade for a typical issuer under an adverse scenario, the agency said. For wealth managers specifically, Fitch identified elevated business model disruption risk as the primary concern. AI-enabled tools could automate or reduce the cost of investment advice, portfolio construction, research support, and advisory execution, according to the report. Commoditisation of advice and the entry of new competitors were cited as the most significant threats, with fee pressure expected to intensify as a result. Fitch drew a distinction between wealth management and private banking, noting that the latter is likely to remain high-touch, with AI augmenting rather than replacing client relationships. Wealth management, by contrast, faces greater exposure to the standardisation of products and services that AI enables. Fiduciary and regulatory obligations requiring human accountability for advice were identified as a key mitigant, limiting full AI substitution, Fitch said. Other mitigants across financial institutions include regulatory barriers to entry, capital requirements, proprietary data, and the capacity to develop in-house AI capabilities. The agency said it does not anticipate AI driving sector-wide rating actions over the next five years for private banking and wealth management issuers, which are likely to moderate AI's competitive impact through greater scale and lower cost to service. title: Human in the loop
excerpt: . We often treat human oversight as the safety net for AI. Let the AI prepare the recommendation and propose the action, and then put a human in the loop to approve it. Problem solved. Except there is one uncomfortable question:. What happens when the human stops reviewing and just starts clicking?. As AI agents take more actions, the number of decisions requiring human approval can grow quickly. A person who receives one unusual request may examine it carefully. A person who receives hundreds of similar requests every day may not. At some point, “human in the loop” can become human just clicking approve. Human oversight is not automatically meaningful oversight. The assumption sounds reasonable: humans provide judgement, context, and accountability that AI lacks. But simply adding a person to a workflow does not guarantee any of those things. NIST has cautioned against assuming that a human overseer will automatically provide effective governance. Human decision-makers bring their own cognitive biases, and the effectiveness of different human-AI configurations depends heavily on how roles and responsibilities are designed. Research also shows how easily people can over-rely on automated recommendations. In one experiment involving 292 participants, people followed algorithmic recommendations more closely than equivalent human recommendations. More importantly, when participants were able to monitor and adjust the automated recommendation, they were less likely to intervene when the algorithm made its largest errors. The researchers concluded that adding a human in the loop increased uptake of automation while decreasing decision accuracy in their experiment. That is automation bias: the tendency to rely too heavily on automated output. The EU AI Act explicitly recognizes this risk. For high-risk AI systems, Article 14 says people responsible for human oversight should be able to understand system limitations, correctly interpret outputs, override or reverse them, and remain aware of the tendency to over-rely on AI-generated recommendations. In other words, the regulator does not consider the mere presence of a human sufficient. The human must actually be capable of challenging the system. In this sense, approval does not always mean a judgement has been made. Imagine an AI agent handling procurement. Most transactions are routine. The agent prepares an action and asks an employee to approve it. Approve. Approve. Approve. Approve. After hundreds of correct recommendations, another approval appears. How carefully does the employee review number 237?. This problem becomes even harder with autonomous agents. A traditional application may require occasional approval. An agent can potentially perform hundreds or thousands of actions as it works toward a goal. OpenID contributors have raised precisely this scalability concern: per-action approval can lead to consent fatigue and reflexive approval, undermining the control it was supposed to provide. So perhaps the question should not be on where we can insert human approval, but where does human judgement genuinely add value? Maybe humans should manage boundaries, not clicks. Meaningful human oversight may require a different model. Instead of asking people to approve every routine action, organizations can define in advance what the agent is allowed to do independently and what requires escalation. For example:. An agent may process standard transactions below a certain risk threshold. But an unusual payment, policy exception, sensitive data access, or action above a defined financial threshold may require human review. The human then focuses attention where judgement matters rather than becoming a bottleneck for thousands of predictable decisions. NIST’s recent work on post-deployment AI monitoring identifies scaling human-driven monitoring as an open challenge and asks how oversight should vary according to risk and use case.
